title: Sustainability and Green Skills
summary: Learn what sustainability means and practise simple energy, water, waste and food calculations. Plan a green project or small business idea with measurable results.
audience: Secondary and university students and young people

body.p: Sustainability means meeting the needs of people today without making it harder for people in the future to meet theirs. It is not only about trees and rivers. Most explanations use three linked parts: the environment (air, water, soil, wildlife and the climate), society (health, fairness, education, safe communities) and the economy (jobs, businesses and the money that lets families live well). A choice is more sustainable when it supports all three, or at least does not damage one badly to help another.

list: Environment: using natural resources at a rate they can recover, and keeping pollution low.
Society: making sure people have fair access to clean water, food, health care and learning, now and later.
Economy: creating work and income that can continue for years, not just a quick profit.

body.p: Imagine a coastal village in Sierra Leone or Ghana where families depend on fishing. If every boat uses very small-mesh nets and takes every fish, income is high for two seasons and then the fish run out. The economy suffers first, then society, because children leave school to look for other work, and the environment is damaged too. If the village agrees on net sizes and rest periods, catches are smaller at first but stay steady for decades. The same thinking applies to a farm in Zambia, a school in Kenya or a city street in London or Madrid.

body.h: Questions to ask about any choice

steps: Who benefits, and who pays the cost, now and later?
Does it use up something that cannot be replaced quickly, such as clean groundwater or fertile soil?
Does it create waste or pollution, and where does that go?
Could it still work in ten years without harming people or nature?
Is there a cheaper, simpler or more local option that does the same job?

body.tip: Sustainability is about trade-offs, not perfection. Aim to make each decision a little better, and be honest about what it costs.

lessons.title: Resources and waste: reduce, reuse, repair, recycle

body.p: Every product, from a school exercise book to a phone, uses materials, energy and water to make and move it. When we throw it away, those resources are lost and the waste must go somewhere. The most useful way to think about waste is as a ladder of actions, with the best actions at the top: refuse and reduce first, then reuse, then repair, then recycle, and only last, dispose.

list: Reduce: do not buy or use what you do not need. Carry a refillable water bottle instead of buying a new sachet or bottle each day.
Reuse: use the same item again for its original or a new purpose. Use both sides of paper, pass on school uniforms and textbooks to a younger student, or use glass jars for storage.
Repair: fix a broken item. A tailor can mend a bag, a phone technician can replace a screen, and a cobbler can resole shoes, which keeps skilled people in work.
Recycle: turn used material into new material, such as metal, glass, paper or some plastics. Recycling needs energy and collection systems, so it comes after the other steps.
Dispose: put the rest in the proper bin or collection point, never in drains, rivers or open burning.

body.h: Worked example: a school tuck shop

body.p: A school tuck shop hands out 120 single-use plastic bags a week. The students propose a deposit scheme for reusable bags and ask customers to bring their own. After a month the shop uses 30 bags a week. The drop is 120 minus 30, which is 90 bags, or about 75 percent less. The numbers also help the school to see whether the idea worked, and to decide what to try next.

Many places have no full recycling service, so learn what your local system accepts. A simple three-bin approach works almost anywhere: food and garden waste (which can be composted), dry materials that might be collected or sold (paper, metal, glass, clean plastic), and everything else. Compost turns vegetable peelings into soil improver, which is a free resource for a school garden. Look up your own town or council rules, because collection services differ a lot between countries.

body.tip: Before you recycle anything, ask: could I have avoided it, reused it or repaired it first?

lessons.title: Energy use at home and school

body.p: Energy is how much work is done, and electricity is measured in watt-hours (Wh) and kilowatt-hours (kWh). A watt (W) is the rate at which a device uses energy. The label on most appliances shows its power in watts. To find the energy used, multiply the power by the hours it runs: watts times hours gives watt-hours. Divide by 1000 to convert to kilowatt-hours. Your electricity bill or prepaid token is based on kWh.

body.code:
energy (Wh)  = power (W) x time (hours)
energy (kWh) = energy (Wh) / 1000
cost         = energy (kWh) x price per kWh

body.p: A fan rated 50 W runs for 8 hours overnight. Energy is 50 x 8 = 400 Wh, which is 0.4 kWh. If we assume a price of 100 currency units per kWh (use your own local price, which you can read on a bill or token receipt), one night costs 40 units.

An old 60 W bulb used for 5 hours a day uses 60 x 5 = 300 Wh, or 0.3 kWh per day. A 10 W LED bulb gives similar light and uses 10 x 5 = 50 Wh, or 0.05 kWh per day. Over 30 days the old bulb uses 9 kWh and costs 900 units at 100 per kWh. The LED uses 1.5 kWh and costs 150 units. The saving is 750 units a month from one bulb. A school with 100 bulbs saves a hundred times as much.

A lab has 20 computers each using 100 W for 6 hours a day. Energy per day is 100 x 6 x 20 = 12000 Wh, which is 12 kWh. At 100 units per kWh that is 1200 units a day. Switching the machines off at the end of the day, rather than leaving them on, is a free saving.

list: Switch off lights, fans and chargers when not needed, and unplug devices that stay warm on standby.
Use daylight: open curtains and place desks near windows.
Choose LED lighting and efficient appliances, and compare the watt rating before you buy.
Cook with lids on pots and use the right size of pan.
Do an energy walk: list devices, their watts and hours, work out kWh, and rank the biggest users.

body.tip: Use big numbers first. A device with high watts or long hours matters more than a phone charger.

lessons.title: Saving water, and thinking about food

body.p: Clean water is limited even in places that seem to have plenty, because it must be collected, cleaned and delivered, which takes energy and money. Saving water protects supply for others and lowers the household bill. The same idea applies to food: growing, transporting and wasting food all use water, land and energy.

list: Turn the tap off while brushing teeth or soaping hands.
Fix dripping taps and leaking pipes quickly.
Collect rainwater from roofs in covered containers for gardens and cleaning, where this is safe and allowed.
Reuse washing-up or laundry water for flushing or watering ornamental plants.
Water plants early morning or evening, when less is lost to evaporation.

body.p: Suppose a tap drips and wastes 1 litre every hour. In a day that is 1 x 24 = 24 litres. In a 30-day month it is 720 litres. A bucket holds about 10 litres, so that is about 72 buckets of clean water lost in a month from a small drip. Compare that with a washing tap left running for 2 minutes at 6 litres a minute: 6 x 2 = 12 litres. Small habits repeated in many homes add up quickly. (These flow rates are assumptions for practice; measure your own with a bucket and a timer.)

Food that is grown nearby usually travels a shorter distance, supports local farmers and traders, and is often fresher. Buying seasonal produce at a local market in Nairobi, Lusaka, Accra or Dublin often means less storage and packaging. Local is not always automatically greener, because the way food is grown also matters, but it is a good starting question. Wasting less food is just as powerful. Plan meals, store food correctly, use leftovers, and compost peelings. A school garden is a practical project: it teaches growing skills, supplies vegetables and uses the compost you make.

body.tip: Check before you act: before starting any rainwater or garden project at school, ask the head teacher and make sure containers are covered to keep mosquitoes out.

lessons.title: Climate and weather in plain terms

body.p: Weather is what the atmosphere is doing now or in the next few days: rain this afternoon, a hot Tuesday, a cold front in the morning. Climate is the pattern of weather in a place over many years, usually a few decades. A simple saying is: weather is your mood today, climate is your personality. One cold day does not disprove a warming climate, just as one hot day does not prove it.

Because weather changes from day to day, scientists look at long records, such as average temperature and rainfall for each month over thirty years or more. The climate of Lagos is hot and humid with a wet and a dry season. The climate of Edinburgh is cool and often cloudy. Both have changing weather. When people discuss climate change they mean long-term shifts in these averages and patterns.

Certain gases in the air, such as carbon dioxide, trap some of the Sun's heat. This natural effect keeps Earth warm enough for life. Burning coal, oil and gas, and clearing forests, adds more of these gases. Scientific bodies around the world study this and explain the link in detail. You do not need advanced science to take useful action, because many actions that cut these gases also save money, such as using less fuel and electricity.

list: Reducing: using less energy, switching to cleaner sources, protecting forests and wasting less.
Adapting: planting drought-resistant crops, building drains that cope with heavy rain, planting shade trees, and making early-warning plans.
Learning: use your national weather service and trusted science sources for local information.

body.p: Worked scenario: a farming community notices that planting dates that worked for their parents now sometimes fail. They keep a simple rainfall diary for the school, then compare years with the weather service. This is local evidence, collected over time, which is the climate-style way of thinking rather than reacting to one storm.

body.tip: When you see a claim about climate, ask whether it is about one event (weather) or a long-term pattern (climate).

body.p: A green job is work that helps protect or restore the environment or uses resources more wisely. Green skills are not only for scientists. Plumbers who fit water-saving taps, electricians who install solar panels, farmers who improve soil, teachers, mechanics, designers and accountants can all work in a greener way.

list: Repair and reuse: phone, shoe, clothes and furniture repair; refurbishing and reselling used items.
Waste services: collecting, sorting and selling clean scrap metal, paper or plastics; composting food waste for gardeners.
Energy: installing and maintaining solar lights and efficient cooking stoves, and doing simple energy checks for shops.
Food: urban gardens, mushroom growing, food preservation, and selling local produce.
Water: rainwater tanks, repair of leaks, and clean-water testing support.
Making: bags from used fabric, refillable soap and cleaning products, reusable sanitary and shopping items.

body.p: Chidi plans to sell liquid soap refills at a market. He buys soap in bulk and sells 50 refills a week. His cost is 12 units a refill and the selling price is 20 units. Profit per refill is 20 minus 12 = 8 units, so weekly profit is 50 x 8 = 400 units before other costs such as transport and rent. He asks customers to bring their own bottle, so he saves packaging, and he can offer a small discount to repeat customers. Before starting he should check the market rules and whether any licence is needed.

steps: Name the problem and the customer: who needs this and why would they pay?
Talk to ten possible customers and listen to their price expectations.
Start small with a trial batch and keep a record of all costs and sales.
Work out your profit per item and your break-even number of sales.
Follow health, safety and local licensing rules, and keep your records honest.

body.tip: Look for a skill you already have plus a local need. You do not need big capital to start a repair or refill service.

lessons.title: Running a clean-up or awareness project

body.p: A project turns good intentions into measurable results. The steps below work for a school club or youth group in any country. As an example, suppose a school club in a town organises a Saturday clean-up of a market area, with 40 volunteers working 2 hours each.

steps: Choose a clear goal, for example: clear the main market lane of litter in one morning and keep it clean for a month.
Get permission from the school, the market or community leaders and the local authority where needed.
Assign roles: team leader, safety lead, sorting team, recorder and photographer.
Prepare supplies: gloves, bags, sturdy shoes, water, first-aid kit. Never ask children to touch sharp objects, medical waste or chemicals.
Arrange where collected waste will go, and sort recyclables if there is a buyer.
Tell the community what you are doing and why, with posters and a short talk.

body.p: Decide what to measure before you start. Total volunteer hours: 40 x 2 = 80 hours. Suppose the group fills 36 bags and each bag weighs about 5 kg on average (weigh a few to estimate). Total waste is 36 x 5 = 180 kg. Per volunteer that is 180 / 40 = 4.5 kg. You can also count the number of items sorted for recycling, take before and after photos from the same place, and do a follow-up check after one month to see whether the litter returned.

list: Share results honestly with the school and community: hours, kilograms and photos.
Ask why the litter was there. Are bins too few or too far apart? A simple fix may do more than repeated clean-ups.
Invite shops and traders to join a regular schedule.
Keep a record of lessons learned for the next group.

body.tip: A small project done well and measured is more convincing than a big one that nobody can describe afterwards.

quiz.q: In sustainability thinking, which three parts are usually considered together?
A village agrees to rest its fishing grounds in some seasons so catches stay steady for decades. Why is this sustainable?
options: It increases the catch every year without limit
It lets the resource recover so income and food continue for future generations
It removes the need for any fishing rules

quiz.q: Which action is highest on the waste ladder?
options: Dispose of it in a bin
Reduce, by not buying what you do not need

quiz.q: A tuck shop cuts plastic bags from 120 a week to 30 a week. What is the percentage reduction, to the nearest whole number?
A 50 W fan runs for 8 hours. How much energy does it use?
A 2000 W kettle runs for 15 minutes (0.25 hours). At an assumed 100 units per kWh, what is the cost?
A computer lab has 20 computers using 100 W each for 6 hours a day. How many kWh per day?
A 60 W bulb is replaced by a 10 W LED. Both are used 5 hours a day for 30 days at 100 units per kWh. What is the monthly saving?
A school wants to find where it wastes the most electricity. What is the best first step?
options: Switch off the main power for a week
List devices with their watts and hours of use, then calculate kWh for each
Count how many bulbs there are and ignore the rest

quiz.q: A tap wastes 1 litre every hour. How many litres does it waste in 30 days?
A cold, snowy week in a city is used as 'proof' that climate is not changing. What is the main flaw?
options: It mixes up short-term weather with long-term climate patterns
Snow can never occur in a changing climate
Climate is measured only in one day
Weather and climate are the same thing

quiz.q: A farming community starts to build better drains for heavier rain and plants drought-tolerant crops. Which response is this?
Chidi sells 50 soap refills a week, costing 12 units each and sold at 20 units. What is his weekly profit before other costs?
A clean-up fills 36 bags averaging 5 kg each, with 40 volunteers. How many kg per volunteer?
After a market clean-up, litter returns within a week. What is the most useful next step?
options: Stop doing clean-ups because they do not work
Find out why, for example too few bins, and fix the cause alongside regular clean-ups
Repeat the same clean-up with no changes forever
